blurb: The most intensely coloured of the hardy sea hollies: branching stems that flood amethyst-violet from the flower cone right down into the upper stem, over leathery, pinnate, spine-edged rosette leaves. A dry limestone-grassland plant that asks for nothing but sun and drainage.
water: Low; dry and lean is ideal — protect it from winter wet, not from drought
spread: Clumping from a taproot; slow and non-running
seasons: Semi-evergreen divided basal rosettes through the cold months; amethyst-blue stems and cones mid-to-late summer; bleached silvery seedheads standing through winter
wildlife: Nectar-rich cones worked by bees, hoverflies and butterflies
toxic: No significant toxicity reported to people or pets; leaves and bracts are leathery and spiny

care.hardiness: The RHS rates it H5 — hardy in most locations even through severe winters — which comfortably covers Boulder's zone 5b–6a, and it is a semi-evergreen perennial rather than a biennial, so an established clump returns for years.[1] The winter risk here is wet, not cold: the RHS is explicit that it needs protection from winter moisture.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall,[4] on a site that drains hard — a slope, a raised bed, a gravel garden or the top of a berm. Like all the taprooted eryngos it transplants poorly and is best sited once and left alone.[1][2] In a container use a gritty, sharply drained mix and keep it under an eave over winter so it does not sit in snowmelt.
care.sun: Full sun is essential.[1] Its whole appeal is the amethyst pigment that floods the bracts and upper stems, and that colour only develops in hard sun; in shade the plant is a floppy green disappointment.
care.soil: Well-drained soil that is poor to moderately fertile — it does well on chalk, loam or sand.[1] Chalk tolerance is the useful signal for us: this is a limestone-grassland plant, so Boulder's alkaline soil suits it exactly.[4] Add grit rather than compost, and never plant it in a bed that is watered like a lawn.[1][3]
care.water: Grow it dry. It wants dry, well-drained ground, and the standard genus guidance is that most sea hollies like very free-draining soil and some thrive in poor, dry soil in sun.[1][2] Water the first season to establish the taproot, then effectively stop; winter wet is what kills it.[1]
care.spacing: Space 12–18 in apart — the RHS gives an ultimate height of roughly 0.5–1 m and a spread of 0.1–0.5 m, so it is a narrow, upright plant that packs in well among low xeric neighbours.[1] Grown lean in full sun it holds itself up.
care.propagation: Root cuttings taken in late winter are the RHS-recommended method and the way to keep a well-coloured plant true.[1] Seed also works; division is a poor choice because of the taproot.[1][2]
care.sow: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall so it takes natural winter chilling, into deep pots or directly where it is to grow. Move seedlings only while very small — once the taproot is down they will not shift.
care.bloom: Flowers in mid-to-late summer, carrying small cylindrical umbels about 2–3 cm long topped by silvery-blue bracts, with the stems themselves colouring light blue to purple.[3] The cones cut and dry superbly and hold their colour better than most sea hollies.
care.feeding: None. Poor to moderately fertile soil is what the RHS specifies; feeding it produces soft, floppy growth and muddier colour.[1]
care.maintenance: Minimal. Flower stems can be cut back after flowering, but the seedheads are a very attractive feature and are usually left over winter — do that here and cut to the ground in early spring.[1] Keep mulch pulled back from the crown so water sheds away from it.
care.selfsow: Modest — it will drop a few seedlings around a happy clump rather than colonising, and volunteers are easy to remove while small. Deadhead before the heads shatter if you want none.
care.troubles: May be susceptible to leaf and bud eelworms, and to slugs and snails; may develop root rot and powdery mildews.[1] Root rot is the one that actually kills plants here, and it is a drainage problem, not a disease you spray.

edible.summary: Grown as an ornamental and a dried flower — Eryngium amethystinum has no documented food use and is not considered dangerously poisonous.[1]
edible.caution: No authority documents this species as edible, so treat it as inedible. The genus does include real foods — the candied 'eryngo' roots of Eryngium maritimum and E. campestre, and culantro (E. foetidum), a culinary herb — but edibility in the carrot family is species-by-species and cannot be inferred from a relative; the same family contains poison hemlock. The real hazard is physical: leathery, spine-edged leaves and bracts that draw blood, so handle and cut it with gloves.[1][3]
